newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman says sure to win Sunday's Croatian poll.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman says sure to win Sunday's Croatian poll.

text.p: Croatia's ailing president Franjo Tudjman, appearing in a pre-election television interview on Wednesday, said that he was sure to win Sunday's presidential election and that his health was excellent.
"(My election victory) is not a question. I am definitely going to win. This is not my own estimate but (Croatian) people are showing me this all the time," the 75-year old president said.
"My victory will perhaps be more overwhelming than before... My two opponents...will together get twice as few votes as me," he said.

He referred to Vlado Gotovac of the Social Liberal party and Zdravko Tomac of the Social Democrats, who will challenge him in Croatia's presidential election on June 15, the second since the former Yugoslav republic gained independence in 1991.

Analysts believe Tudjman will win outright in the first round, but they doubt he will live out his second five-year term in office. He is alleged to be suffering from cancer and was treated in a U.S. hospital last November.

But Tudjman, who looked well and appeared to have gained some weight, sought to put an end to such rumours. "I work ten, 12 to 16 hours a day, I play tennis twice a week to stay fit. I think my condition is excellent," he said.
The president brushed aside Western criticism of his undemocratic rule and too tight a grip on media.
"I think there are a thousand independent media in Croatia. The media are free, democracy means everybody can speak their minds but it doesn't mean irresponsibility and anarchy," he said.

The Croatian government controls almost all daily papers and the state radio. The television, from which most Croats get their daily news, is perceived as a mere mouthpiece for Tudjman's ruling HDZ (Croatian Democratic Union) party.
Asked if he would allow a countrywide private television network, Tudjman said: "Yes, but not (one) in the service of foreign interests but of Croatian people."
He added that Croatia was faced with a psychological warfare waged by domestic and international forces.
"We are facing an organised activity, including psychological war, aimed at obstructing our independence, waged by a lot of people in Croatia and abroad, who cannot accept Croatia's sovereignty".
In their campaigns his rivals Gotovac and Tomac charged that the power and wealth were concentrated in the hands of the HDZ only and said it was time to change it.
Tudjman said such allegations about corruption and quick enrichment of the HDZ government members were part of the psychological warfare, aimed at destabilising the country.
"It is of vital importance that Croatia pursues the policy with which it secured its liberty," he said.
